Deprecated SDK imports removed¶

This project no longer depends on bigdata-client or bigdata-research-tools. See MIGRATION_NOTES.md / README.md and Thematic_Screener_CLI for the REST + bigdata-smart-batching + OpenAI pattern. Pass company CSVs (RP_ENTITY_ID, COMPANY_NAME) instead of watchlists.

Regulatory Issues in the Tech Sector Report Generator¶

Automated Analysis of Regulatory Risks and Company Mitigation Strategies¶

Why It Matters¶

Technology companies face an increasingly complex regulatory landscape spanning AI governance, data privacy, antitrust scrutiny, and platform accountability. Tracking compliance risks across multiple companies and jurisdictions manually is time-consuming and fragmented, while regulatory developments appear scattered across news coverage, SEC filings, and earnings transcripts.

What It Does¶

The GenerateReport class in the bigdata-research-tools package systematically analyzes regulatory exposure across company watchlists using unstructured data from news, filings, and transcripts. Built for risk managers and investment professionals, it transforms scattered regulatory information into quantifiable risk intelligence and identifies proactive company mitigation strategies.

How It Works¶

The Report Generator combines automated theme taxonomies, multi-source content retrieval, and LLM-powered risk scoring to deliver:

  • Sector-wide regulatory mapping across technology domains (AI, Social Media, Hardware & Chips, E-commerce, Advertising)
  • Company-specific risk quantification using Media Attention, Risk/Financial Impact, and Uncertainty metrics
  • Mitigation strategy extraction from corporate communications to identify compliance approaches
  • Structured output for reporting ranking regulatory issues by intensity and business impact

A Real-World Use Case¶

This cookbook demonstrates the complete workflow through analyzing regulatory challenges across the "Magnificent 7" tech companies, showing how the generator automatically creates comprehensive risk assessments and extracts company response strategies from multiple document sources.

Setup and Imports¶

Async Compatibility Setup¶

Run this cell first - Required for Google Colab, Jupyter Notebooks, and VS Code with Jupyter extension:

Why is this needed?¶

Interactive environments (Colab, Jupyter) already have an asyncio event loop running. When bigdata-research-tools makes async API calls (like to OpenAI), you'll get this error without nest_asyncio:

RuntimeError: asyncio.run() cannot be called from a running event loop

The nest_asyncio.apply() command patches this to allow nested event loops.

💡 Tip: If you're unsure which environment you're in, just run the cell below - it won't hurt in any environment!

In [1]:
import datetime
start = datetime.datetime.now()

try:
    import asyncio
    asyncio.get_running_loop()
    import nest_asyncio; nest_asyncio.apply()
    print("✅ nest_asyncio applied")
except (RuntimeError, ImportError):
    print("✅ nest_asyncio not needed or not available")

✅ nest_asyncio applied

Defining the Report Parameters¶

Fixed Parameters¶

  • General Theme (general_theme): The central regulatory concept to explore across all technology domains
  • Specific Focus Areas (list_specific_focus): Technology sectors where regulatory issues are particularly relevant
  • Bigdata (bigdata): Bigdata connection

Customizable Parameters¶

  • Watchlist (my_watchlist_id): The set of companies to analyze. This is the ID of your watchlist in https://app.bigdata.com/watchlists
  • Model Selection (llm_model): The LLM model used to label search result document chunks and generate summaries
  • Frequency (search_frequency): The frequency of the date ranges to search over. Supported values:
    • Y: Yearly intervals
    • M: Monthly intervals
    • W: Weekly intervals
    • D: Daily intervals. Defaults to M
  • Time Period (start_date and end_date): The date range over which to run the analysis
  • Fiscal Year (fiscal_year): If the document type is transcripts or filings, fiscal year needs to be specified
  • Focus (focus): Specify a focus within the main theme. This will then be used in building the LLM generated mindmapper
  • Document Limits (document_limit_news, document_limit_filings, document_limit_transcripts): The maximum number of documents to return per query to Bigdata API for each category of documents
  • Batch Size (batch_size): The number of entities to include in a single batched query
In [7]:
# ===== Fixed Parameters =====

# General regulatory theme
general_theme = 'Regulatory Issues'

# Specific focus areas within technology sectors.
# Cost control: trimmed from 5 to 2 focus areas for this real, billed run.
list_specific_focus = ['AI', 'Social Media', 'Hardware and Chips', 'E-commerce', 'Advertising']
In [8]:
# ===== Customizable Parameters =====

# Company Universe — loaded from a CSV (RP_ENTITY_ID, COMPANY_NAME) instead of
# a platform watchlist. mag7.csv already matches the "Magnificent 7" companies
# this notebook was originally built around.
# Cost control: keep the executed universe small (~5 companies).
universe_path = "../Thematic_Screener_CLI/mag7.csv"
universe_df = load_universe(universe_path)
company_ids = company_ids_from_universe(universe_df)
id_to_name = dict(zip(universe_df["RP_ENTITY_ID"], universe_df["COMPANY_NAME"]))
company_names = universe_df["COMPANY_NAME"].tolist()

# Downstream summarizers expect objects with .id / .name attributes.
companies = [SimpleNamespace(id=entity_id, name=name) for entity_id, name in id_to_name.items()]

# LLM Specification
llm_model = "gpt-5.6-luna"

# Search Frequency (kept for compatibility; unused by the REST search helper)
search_frequency = 'M'

# Specify Time Range — cost control: narrow ~30 day window
end_date = "2025-04-20"
start_date = "2025-01-01"

# Fiscal Year
fiscal_year = 2025

# Document Limits (kept for compatibility with GenerateReport's signature)
document_limit_news = 10
document_limit_filings = 10
document_limit_transcripts = 5

# Others
batch_size = 1

print(f"Universe: {len(company_ids)} companies -> {company_names}")
print(f"Date window: {start_date} to {end_date}")

Workflow step by step¶

Mindmap a Theme Taxonomy with Bigdata Research Tools¶

You can leverage Bigdata Research Tools to generate a comprehensive theme taxonomy with an LLM, breaking down a megatrend into smaller, well-defined concepts for more targeted analysis.

In [10]:
# Generate the Theme Tree (plain OpenAI-based taxonomy; replaces the removed
# bigdata-research-tools mindmap generator, same terminal-label/summary shape)
themes_tree_dict = {}
for focus in list_specific_focus:
    theme_tree = generate_theme_tree(
                        main_theme=general_theme,
                        focus=focus
                    )
    themes_tree_dict[focus] = theme_tree

# ThemeTree has no .visualize() (that was a bigdata-research-tools/graphviz
# feature) — print the leaf labels + summaries instead.
for focus, tree in themes_tree_dict.items():
    print(f"\n=== {focus} ===")
    for label, summary in tree.get_terminal_label_summaries().items():
        print(f"- {label}: {summary}")

=== AI ===
- Risk Classification and Compliance Obligations: Regulatory Issues concerning AI include risk-based classification requirements that determine the compliance obligations for different artificial intelligence applications.
- Transparency and Explainability: Regulatory Issues concerning AI include requirements for transparency, documentation, and explainability of artificial intelligence systems and their decisions.
- Privacy and Data Protection: Regulatory Issues concerning AI include privacy, data protection, consent, and lawful data-use requirements for training and operating artificial intelligence systems.
- Safety, Bias, and Discrimination: Regulatory Issues concerning AI include requirements to manage safety risks, algorithmic bias, and discriminatory impacts produced by artificial intelligence systems.

=== Social Media ===
- Misinformation and Disinformation: Regulatory Issues in Social Media include obligations and enforcement challenges related to preventing the spread of misinformation and disinformation.
- Harmful and Illegal Content: Regulatory Issues in Social Media include requirements for identifying, reporting, restricting, and removing harmful or illegal content.
- Data Privacy and Consent: Regulatory Issues in Social Media include rules governing the collection, processing, sharing, and consent-based use of personal data.
- Child Protection and Online Safety: Regulatory Issues in Social Media include measures designed to protect children and vulnerable users from exploitation, abuse, and unsafe platform features.
- Algorithmic Transparency: Regulatory Issues in Social Media include requirements for transparency, risk assessment, and oversight of recommender systems and algorithmic decision-making.
- Advertising and Influencer Disclosure: Regulatory Issues in Social Media include rules requiring clear disclosure of sponsored content, targeted advertising, and commercial relationships involving influencers.

=== Hardware and Chips ===
- Export Controls and Sanctions: Regulatory Issues concerning export controls, sanctions, and licensing requirements for semiconductors, chip-design tools, and advanced manufacturing equipment.
- Supply Chain Due Diligence: Regulatory Issues concerning traceability, origin disclosure, conflict-mineral compliance, and forced-labor screening across hardware and semiconductor supply chains.
- Product Safety and Certification: Regulatory Issues concerning electrical safety, electromagnetic compatibility, radio approvals, and mandatory certification for hardware devices and components.
- Cybersecurity and Product Security: Regulatory Issues concerning secure-by-design requirements, vulnerability disclosure, software updates, and cybersecurity standards for connected hardware and chips.
- Hazardous Materials and E-Waste: Regulatory Issues concerning restrictions on hazardous substances, recycling obligations, producer responsibility, and e-waste management for hardware and chips.

=== E-commerce ===
- Advertising, Pricing, and Disclosures: Regulatory issues in e-commerce include requirements for truthful advertising, transparent pricing, product claims, and clear disclosure of material terms.
- Returns, Refunds, and Product Safety: Regulatory issues in e-commerce include consumer rights concerning returns, refunds, warranties, recalls, and the safety of products sold online.
- Privacy and Data Protection: Regulatory issues in e-commerce include privacy notices, consent requirements, consumer data rights, cross-border transfers, and protection of personal information.
- Cybersecurity and Online Identity: Regulatory issues in e-commerce include cybersecurity safeguards, breach notification duties, identity verification, and controls against account takeover and fraud.
- Payments, Taxes, and Financial Compliance: Regulatory issues in e-commerce include payment processing, sales tax and VAT collection, consumer credit, anti-money-laundering controls, and financial disclosures.
- Platforms, Competition, and Seller Governance: Regulatory issues in e-commerce include marketplace liability, competition rules, platform transparency, seller verification, content moderation, and oversight of dominant digital platforms.

=== Advertising ===
- Truthfulness and Substantiation: Regulatory Issues in Advertising include requirements that claims be truthful, accurate, and supported by reliable evidence.
- Disclosures and Transparency: Regulatory Issues in Advertising include requirements for clear disclosures about sponsorships, material connections, pricing, limitations, and other relevant information.
- Children and Vulnerable Audiences: Regulatory Issues in Advertising include restrictions and safeguards for advertising directed at children or other vulnerable audiences.
- Privacy and Targeted Advertising: Regulatory Issues in Advertising include rules governing the collection and use of personal data for behavioral, targeted, and personalized advertising.
- Comparative and Competitive Advertising: Regulatory Issues in Advertising include requirements that comparative claims be fair, verifiable, and not misleading toward competitors or consumers.

The taxonomy tree includes descriptive sentences that explicitly connect each sub-theme back to the Regulatory Issues general theme, ensuring all search results remain contextually relevant to our central trend.

Retrieve Content¶

With the theme taxonomy and screening parameter you can leverage the Bigdata API to run a search on company news, filings and transcripts.

In [11]:
# Run searches on News, Filings, and Transcripts via the Bigdata REST +
# smart-batching stack (replaces removed bigdata-research-tools search_by_companies)
df_sentences_news = []
df_sentences_filings = []
df_sentences_transcripts = []

scopes_config = [
    ("news", df_sentences_news, document_limit_news),
    ("filings", df_sentences_filings, document_limit_filings),
    ("transcripts", df_sentences_transcripts, document_limit_transcripts),
]

CHUNK_PERCENTAGE = 0.01

for scope, df_list, doc_limit in scopes_config:
    if doc_limit <= 0:
        continue
    for focus in list_specific_focus:
        theme_summaries = list(themes_tree_dict[focus].get_terminal_label_summaries().values())
        df_sentences = run_universe_search(
            company_ids=company_ids,
            queries=theme_summaries,
            start_date=start_date,
            end_date=end_date,
            scope=scope,
            chunk_percentage=CHUNK_PERCENTAGE,
            document_limit_per_query=doc_limit,
            id_to_name=id_to_name,
        )
        if df_sentences.empty:
            df_sentences = pd.DataFrame(columns=SEARCH_COLUMNS)
        df_sentences['theme'] = general_theme + ' in ' + focus
        df_list.append(df_sentences)

# Concatenate results
df_sentences_news = pd.concat(df_sentences_news, ignore_index=True) if df_sentences_news else pd.DataFrame(columns=SEARCH_COLUMNS)
df_sentences_filings = pd.concat(df_sentences_filings, ignore_index=True) if df_sentences_filings else pd.DataFrame(columns=SEARCH_COLUMNS)
df_sentences_transcripts = pd.concat(df_sentences_transcripts, ignore_index=True) if df_sentences_transcripts else pd.DataFrame(columns=SEARCH_COLUMNS)

print(f"news={len(df_sentences_news)} filings={len(df_sentences_filings)} transcripts={len(df_sentences_transcripts)}")

Label the Results¶

Use an LLM to analyze each document chunk and determine its relevance to the main theme. Any document chunks which aren't explicitly linked to Regulatory Issues will be filtered out.

In [15]:
# Label the search results with our theme labels
labeler = SimpleLabeler(model=llm_model.split('::')[-1] if '::' in llm_model else llm_model, api_key=OPENAI_API_KEY)

# Initialize empty lists for labeled data
df_news_labeled = []
df_filings_labeled = []
df_transcripts_labeled = []

# Configure data sources
sources_config = [
    (df_sentences_news, df_news_labeled),
    (df_sentences_filings, df_filings_labeled),
    (df_sentences_transcripts, df_transcripts_labeled),
]

# Cap OpenAI labeling calls per theme/scope combination
MAX_ROWS_TO_LABEL = 50

for df_sentences, labeled_list in sources_config:
    for focus in list_specific_focus:
        df_sentences_theme = df_sentences.loc[(df_sentences.theme == general_theme + ' in ' + focus)]
        df_sentences_theme = df_sentences_theme.reset_index(drop=True).head(MAX_ROWS_TO_LABEL)
        if df_sentences_theme.empty:
            continue
        df_labels = labeler.get_labels(
            main_theme=general_theme + ' in ' + focus,
            labels=list(themes_tree_dict[focus].get_terminal_label_summaries().keys()),
            texts=df_sentences_theme["masked_text"].tolist()
        )
        df_merged_labels = pd.merge(df_sentences_theme, df_labels, left_index=True, right_index=True)
        labeled_list.append(df_merged_labels)

# Concatenate results
df_news_labeled = pd.concat(df_news_labeled, ignore_index=True) if df_news_labeled else pd.DataFrame(columns=LABEL_COLUMNS)
df_filings_labeled = pd.concat(df_filings_labeled, ignore_index=True) if df_filings_labeled else pd.DataFrame(columns=LABEL_COLUMNS)
df_transcripts_labeled = pd.concat(df_transcripts_labeled, ignore_index=True) if df_transcripts_labeled else pd.DataFrame(columns=LABEL_COLUMNS)

print(f"labeled: news={len(df_news_labeled)} filings={len(df_filings_labeled)} transcripts={len(df_transcripts_labeled)}")

Document Distribution Visualization¶

You can visualize the tables showing the count of different document types for each company in the given universe. This helps you understand the distribution and availability of information across different sources for each entity.

In [16]:
df_statistic_resources = pd.concat([df_news_labeled, df_filings_labeled, df_transcripts_labeled])

create_styled_table(df_statistic_resources,title='Retrieved Document Count by Company and Document Type', companies_list = company_names)
In [17]:
df_statistic_resources_relevant = df_statistic_resources.loc[~df_statistic_resources.label.isin(['', 'unassigned', 'unclear'])]
create_styled_table(df_statistic_resources_relevant, title='Relevant Document Count by Company and Document Type', companies_list = company_names)

Summarizer¶

The following code is used to create a summary for each company using the information from the retrieved documents.

In [18]:
# Run the process to summarize the documents and compute media attention by topic, sector-wide
summarizer_sector = TopicSummarizerSector(
   model=llm_model.split('::')[-1] if '::' in llm_model else llm_model,
   api_key=OPENAI_API_KEY,
   df_labeled=df_news_labeled,
   general_theme=general_theme,
   list_specific_focus=list_specific_focus,
   themes_tree_dict=themes_tree_dict,
   logger=GenerateReport.logger
)
df_by_theme = summarizer_sector.summarize()
if df_by_theme is None:
    df_by_theme = pd.DataFrame(columns=['theme', 'topic', 'topic_summary', 'n_documents'])

# Run the process to summarize the documents and score media attention, risk and uncertainty by topic at company level
summarizer_company = TopicSummarizerCompany(
   model=llm_model.split('::')[-1] if '::' in llm_model else llm_model,
   api_key=OPENAI_API_KEY,
   logger=GenerateReport.logger,
   verbose=True
)
df_by_company = asyncio.run(
   summarizer_company.process_topic_by_company(
       df_labeled=df_news_labeled,
       list_entities=companies
   )
)
if df_by_company is None or df_by_company.empty:
    df_by_company = pd.DataFrame(columns=[
        'entity_id', 'entity_name', 'topic', 'topic_summary', 'risk_magnitude', 'risk_summary',
        'uncertainty', 'uncertainty_explanation', 'n_documents', 'risk_score', 'uncertainty_score',
    ])

print(f"df_by_theme: {len(df_by_theme)} rows, df_by_company: {len(df_by_company)} rows")

Company Response Analysis¶

Extract company mitigation strategies from filings and transcripts.

In [19]:
# Concatenate Filings and Transcripts dataframes
df_filings_labeled['doc_type'] = 'Filings'
df_transcripts_labeled['doc_type'] = 'Transcripts'
df_ft_labeled = pd.concat([df_filings_labeled, df_transcripts_labeled])
df_ft_labeled = df_ft_labeled.reset_index(drop=True)

# Run the process to extract company's mitigation plan from the documents (filings and transcripts)
response_processor = CompanyResponseProcessor(
   model=llm_model.split('::')[-1] if '::' in llm_model else llm_model,
   api_key=OPENAI_API_KEY,
   logger=GenerateReport.logger,
   verbose=True
)


df_response_by_company = asyncio.run(
   response_processor.process_response_by_company(
       df_labeled=df_ft_labeled,
       df_by_company=df_by_company,
       list_entities=companies
   )
)

# Merge the companies responses to the dataframe with issue summaries and scores
df_by_company_with_responses = pd.merge(df_by_company, df_response_by_company, on=['entity_id', 'entity_name', 'topic'], how='left')
df_by_company_with_responses['filings_response_summary'] = df_by_company_with_responses['response_summary']

# Extract the company's mitigation plan for each regulatory issue from the News documents
df_news_response_by_company = asyncio.run(
   response_processor.process_response_by_company(
       df_labeled=df_news_labeled,
       df_by_company=df_by_company,
       list_entities=companies
   )
)

df_news_response_by_company = df_news_response_by_company.rename(
   columns={'response_summary': 'news_response_summary', 'n_response_documents': 'news_n_response_documents'}
)
df_by_company_with_responses = pd.merge(df_by_company_with_responses, df_news_response_by_company,
                                       on=['entity_id', 'entity_name', 'topic'], how='left')
df_by_company_with_responses['response_summary'] = df_by_company_with_responses['response_summary'].fillna(
   df_by_company_with_responses['news_response_summary']
)


report_by_theme = df_by_theme
report_by_company = df_by_company_with_responses

Direct method¶

Once the class GenerateReport is initialized you can just run the method generate_report() to get the final output and then you can run the functions to visualize the results and to generate the report.

For practical reasons you can also choose to import and/or export the intermediate outputs to/from a specific directory:

  • import_from_path: File path from where the intermediate outputs will be loaded
  • export_to_path: File path where the intermediate outputs will be saved

To run the direct method uncomment the variable DIRECT_METHOD

To export the intermediate results / final outputs uncomment the variable EXPORT_RESULTS

In [20]:
# Uncomment the flag DIRECT_METHOD to run the workflow
#DIRECT_METHOD_FLAG = True
#EXPORT_RESULTS_FLAG = True

if 'DIRECT_METHOD_FLAG' in globals() and DIRECT_METHOD_FLAG:
  if 'EXPORT_RESULTS_FLAG' in globals() and EXPORT_RESULTS_FLAG:
    report = report_generator.generate_report(import_from_path=output_dir, export_to_path=output_dir)
  else:
    report = report_generator.generate_report()

  themes_tree_dict=report.themes_tree_dict
  df_by_theme=report.report_by_theme
  df_by_company_with_responses=report.report_by_company

Generate Final Report¶

Rank the topics based on their Media Attention, Risk/Financial Impact, and Uncertainty.

You can customize the ranking system by specifying the number of top themes to display (user_selected_nb_topics_themes).

The report will provide a detailed analysis of individual companies, highlighting three key aspects:

  1. Most Reported Issue
  2. Biggest Risk
  3. Most Uncertain Issue

Each aspect is analyzed using its own ranking system, allowing for a tailored and detailed view of company-specific topics.

In [21]:
# generate the html report
top_by_theme, top_by_company = prepare_data_report_0(
     df_by_theme = df_by_theme,
     df_by_company_with_responses = df_by_company_with_responses,
     user_selected_nb_topics_themes = 3,
)

html_content = generate_html_report(top_by_theme, top_by_company, 'Regulatory Issues in the Tech Sector')

with open(output_dir+'/report.html', 'w') as file:
     file.write(html_content)

display(HTML(html_content))
Regulatory Issues in the Tech Sector

Regulatory Issues in the Tech Sector

August 27, 2026

Sector-Wide Issues

Regulatory Issues in AI

  • Risk Classification and Compliance Obligations: AI governance frameworks increasingly classify systems by risk, with the EU AI Act cited as categorizing applications and restricting high-risk uses such as biometric surveillance; Meta’s Frontier AI Framework similarly contemplates halting systems assessed as presenting “critical risk,” although its classifications rely on expert reviews because quantitative evaluation remains limited. Compliance obligations highlighted across the reports include risk and safety assessments, transparency and explainability, bias mitigation, accountability and traceability, privacy compliance under measures such as GDPR, and reporting requirements—obligations that could become costly and fragmented across the 50 different state standards anticipated in the United States; the revocation of the 2023 Biden executive order also removed requirements for new safety assessments, equity and civil-rights guidance, and labor-market research.
  • Privacy and Data Protection: AI regulation is increasingly focused on lawful, transparent collection and processing of personal, biometric, medical, children’s and training data, with requirements for clear consent, user control, data minimization, encryption, deletion, age verification and accountability. Enforcement includes the Dutch Data Protection Authority’s €30.5 million fine against Clearview AI in 2024, Italy’s €15 million fine against OpenAI for GDPR breaches in 2024, and the FTC’s $25 million fine against Amazon in 2023 for retaining children’s Alexa recordings; meanwhile, a U.S. executive order in 2025 rescinded Biden-era AI safety and transparency requirements, while concerns remain over data scraping, AI training practices and the privacy risks of consumer devices.
  • Transparency and Explainability: Across the reports, transparency and explainability are presented as essential to AI safety, trust, accountability and bias mitigation: companies such as Google, OpenAI, IBM and Microsoft support labeling AI-generated content, explainable AI, documentation of algorithms and data sources, and visibility throughout the AI life cycle. Regulatory frameworks may require disclosure of decision-making processes and training-data quality, traceability, regular fairness and compliance audits, and human oversight, although complex agentic systems using constantly changing real-time data and opaque “black-box” models make decisions difficult to document or explain, particularly in high-stakes sectors.

Regulatory Issues in Advertising

  • Truthfulness and Substantiation: Regulatory scrutiny consistently emphasizes that advertising must be truthful, accurate, and supported by evidence: the National Advertising Division has monitored national advertising since 1971 and offers expedited or complex substantiation reviews, while ASIC requires product risks, returns, liquidity, and advertising methods such as domain names and Google Ads to be represented truthfully. The ASA ruled in March that Haven Leisure Ltd’s holiday price claims were misleading and unsubstantiated under CAP Code Rule 3, and regulators’ increasing use of AI is raising detection and compliance risks; medicines guidance likewise permits factual information but not product claims without appropriate support.
  • Privacy and Targeted Advertising: Regulatory scrutiny is increasingly limiting the use of personal and cross-site data for targeted advertising: California’s proposed AI decision-making rules could cost advertisers $20,000 or more, while the EU has required restrictions on data collected from other websites and rejected Meta’s subscription-based ad model as unlawful. Privacy concerns have also led to the GDPR and CCPA, two lawsuits alleging The Trade Desk’s UID2 violates the CCPA, and major enforcement against Meta, including the FTC’s $5 billion fine in 2019 and an EU fine of nearly EUR800 million in November.
  • Comparative and Competitive Advertising: US District Judge Leonie Brinkema ruled that Google willfully acquired and maintained illegal monopoly power in the open-web display publisher ad-server and ad-exchange markets, and unlawfully tied those products, while the government failed to prove monopolization of advertiser ad networks. The antitrust findings, brought by the US government and multiple states under the Sherman Act, could lead to divestiture of Google Ad Manager, including AdX and DFP, or behavioral remedies such as banning Google from favoring its own exchange, amid findings that its conduct restricted rivals, harmed publishers, competition and consumers.

Regulatory Issues in E-commerce

  • Platforms, Competition, and Seller Governance: eBay’s 2024 Form 10-K highlights intensifying competition from larger platforms including Alibaba, Google, Amazon, Apple and Meta, while sellers increasingly use multiple channels and must meet higher expectations for shipping, returns and service. Regulatory scrutiny is targeting platform power and conduct: the EU DMA reviews Google’s self-preferencing and Google Play fees, challenged Meta’s integration of Marketplace and data advantages, and requires Apple to improve interoperability and access for developers and device makers; Australia’s ACCC is developing service-specific codes by March 2025 covering interoperability, transparency and fair dealing with business users. These measures may constrain proprietary ecosystems, self-preferencing, exclusive arrangements and platform operations, while increasing compliance costs and requiring more predictable treatment and access for sellers, developers and other business users.
  • Advertising, Pricing, and Disclosures: E-commerce regulation is shaped by inconsistent country-level taxes, financial obligations, sellable-item restrictions, and potential stricter consumer-protection rules, creating pricing and compliance uncertainty for platforms and sellers. Digital advertising faces ad fraud, brand-safety concerns, rising placement costs, and competition from platform-owned advertising media, while disclosures and data-protection obligations are highlighted by the Business Standard personal-views disclaimer and authID’s January 2025 emphasis on biometric privacy compliance and storing no biometric data.
  • Privacy and Data Protection: Privacy concerns in e-commerce and connected-device ecosystems center on limiting data collection, protecting personal information, and securing data through measures such as advanced encryption; Google Home users are advised to adjust settings to safeguard privacy and share as little data as possible with Google. Data privacy is a major regulatory focus for platforms including Amazon, Google, Meta, X, Alibaba, and Tencent, with the GDPR—implemented in 2018 and associated with $1.3 billion in fines in 2024—driving similar but nationally varied laws worldwide.

Regulatory Issues in Hardware and Chips

  • Export Controls and Sanctions: U.S. export controls on advanced AI chips and semiconductor-manufacturing technology aimed at China expanded from the October 2022 restrictions on Nvidia’s A100/H100 to the October 2023 ban on A800/H800, rules effective April 2024, further controls in December 2024, and 2025 licensing requirements for Nvidia’s H20 and AMD’s MI308; proposed measures would also require licenses for chips at 14/16 nanometers and below and impose stronger customer due diligence on TSMC, Samsung, and Intel. The restrictions have halted or limited shipments and created major financial exposure—including Nvidia’s approximately $5.5 billion charge—while reports say they may accelerate Huawei and other Chinese alternatives, encourage workarounds and domestic innovation, and reduce U.S. companies’ market access and competitiveness.
  • Cybersecurity and Product Security: Regulatory and product-security efforts emphasize secure-by-design hardware and connected products, including NIST IoT criteria for unique identification, secure configuration, data protection, access control, verified software updates, incident awareness, documentation, and timely vulnerability disclosures. Microsoft’s February 2025 remediation of GRUB2, U-Boot, and Barebox flaws—some enabling arbitrary code execution or Secure Boot bypass—highlights bootloader and hardware-platform risks, while ISO/IEC 27001, NIST, CIS, and FFIEC frameworks support compliance, data protection, and security validation amid broader regulatory concerns over privacy, cyber threats, and supply-chain dependencies.
  • Product Safety and Certification: Alphabet disclosed risks that device quality defects stemming from design, manufacturing, operations, or suppliers could lead to recalls, reputational damage, and financial harm, while requiring suppliers to follow applicable laws and its Google Supplier Code of Conduct. On January 7, 2025, the U.S. National Highway Traffic Safety Administration’s Office of Defects Investigation examined Tesla’s Smart Summon and Actually Smart Summon features after four reported crashes involving undetected objects or parked vehicles and 12 additional Smart Summon-related crashes; the agency also said Tesla had not reported crashes as required for incidents on public roads.

Regulatory Issues in Social Media

  • Misinformation and Disinformation: Reports describe growing concern that relaxed moderation, removal of third-party fact-checkers and algorithmic echo chambers on platforms such as Meta, X, TikTok and YouTube could allow misinformation and disinformation—including COVID-19, political and cross-platform false narratives—to spread more rapidly and undermine trust. Regulatory responses are diverging: the EU’s 2022 Digital Services Act requires platforms to mitigate disinformation and allows fines of up to 6% of global annual revenue, while the UK launched an algorithm and misinformation inquiry on February 20, 2025; meanwhile, measures in Vietnam requiring removal of illegal posts within 24 hours and alleged government pressure over COVID-19 content have intensified debates over censorship, accountability and free expression.
  • Data Privacy and Consent: The draft Digital Personal Data Protection Rules released on January 3 require verifiable parental consent before processing children’s data or creating their social-media accounts, while potentially imposing data-localisation and cross-border-sharing oversight; companies warn that compliance mechanisms remain unsettled and may advantage data-rich platforms such as Google and Meta over smaller firms. More broadly, GDPR-style opt-in requirements, concerns about opaque data collection and user control, and Apple’s $95 million Siri settlement highlight growing demands for transparency, meaningful consent, and stronger safeguards for personal data.
  • Child Protection and Online Safety: Regulatory efforts to protect children online intensified in 2024, led by Australia’s November 2024 law barring under-16s from social media and requiring platforms to take reasonable enforcement steps, with reported fines of up to A$50 million (about US$31 million) or $32 million; Indonesia is considering similar age limits and interim child-protection guidelines amid concerns over exploitation, radical content and harmful material. Reports also highlight risks from bullying, sexual exploitation, blackmail, misinformation, body-image pressures and trolling, while India and European countries consider tighter controls; however, advocates warn that age verification and expanded monitoring may create privacy and surveillance concerns, especially as Meta removes fact-checkers.

Company-Specific Issues

Alphabet Inc.

1. Most Reported Issue
Regulatory Issues in Social Media - Misinformation and Disinformation: Alphabet faces intensifying regulation over misinformation and disinformation, including UK scrutiny of Google’s search and AI features on 20 February 2025, congressional demands for communications about alleged government pressure on YouTube’s COVID-19 content decisions, EU Digital Services Act content-moderation enforcement, Vietnam’s requirements for Google/YouTube to remove illegal posts within 24 hours and enable official access, and heightened antitrust exposure following the U.S. Department of Justice’s 2024 digital-advertising lawsuit victory and the expected 2025 outcome of Google’s second case.
[14 News]
2. Biggest Risk
Regulatory Issues in E-commerce - Platforms, Competition, and Seller Governance: Alphabet faces high regulatory risk because EU authorities preliminarily found Google Search favoring its own services and Google Play restricting steering while charging potentially unjustified fees, which could require costly business and product changes and materially affect its operations and revenue.
[7 News]
3. Most Uncertain Issue
Regulatory Issues in E-commerce - Advertising, Pricing, and Disclosures: The reports mention Google advertising and Google as a digital gatekeeper but do not specify how e-commerce advertising, pricing, or disclosure regulations will directly affect Alphabet, leaving the outcome highly uncertain.
[3 News]

Company's Response:
  • Regulatory Issues in Social Media - Misinformation and Disinformation: Alphabet states that it may modify Google Search and YouTube, strengthen content-moderation and algorithm-disclosure practices, and incur additional costs to operate and monitor minors’ experiences in response to laws including the EU Digital Services Act, while its separate agreement with Reddit licenses Reddit’s conversation corpus to Google for training large language models.
  • Regulatory Issues in E-commerce - Platforms, Competition, and Seller Governance: The reports disclose no specific mitigation plan or regulatory response from Alphabet; they only reference Google Shopping and Google’s Gemini AI engine as channels through which consumers may search, while noting that Digital Markets Act investigations could change how companies interact with Google.
  • Regulatory Issues in E-commerce - Advertising, Pricing, and Disclosures: Alphabet’s response is reflected in continued development of Google’s Gemini AI engine as a potential evolution of search, while Google Cloud is offered alongside Azure, AWS, and IBM Cloud in customers’ multi-cloud deployments, supporting continued access to Google’s services as regulatory and governance requirements evolve.

Amazon.com Inc.

1. Most Reported Issue
Regulatory Issues in Hardware and Chips - Export Controls and Sanctions: Amazon.com’s supply chain has reportedly been compromised by malicious microchips, while new U.S. controls on advanced AI-chip exports to 120 countries create additional compliance challenges for Amazon as a major cloud provider, and China’s retaliatory tariffs have prompted Amazon to cancel some China orders and could raise U.S. prices.
[6 News]
2. Biggest Risk
Regulatory Issues in Hardware and Chips - Export Controls and Sanctions: Export controls and sanctions create compliance challenges for Amazon’s cloud and AI-chip activities, while reported supply-chain compromises and China-related tariffs could increase operational and cost risks, indicating a medium potential financial impact.
[6 News]
3. Most Uncertain Issue
Regulatory Issues in E-commerce - Advertising, Pricing, and Disclosures: The report only identifies Amazon as an alternative e-commerce marketplace for eBay users and provides no information about how advertising, pricing, or disclosure regulations would affect Amazon.
[1 News]

Company's Response:
  • Regulatory Issues in Hardware and Chips - Export Controls and Sanctions: Amazon’s reported response includes unveiling its Ocelot quantum chip and committing to support the 2025 Cyber Trust Mark program by highlighting products that meet NIST cybersecurity criteria, while the reports provide no further company-specific details on supply-chain traceability or export-control compliance.
  • Regulatory Issues in E-commerce - Advertising, Pricing, and Disclosures: In its February 6–7, 2025 filings and earnings materials, Amazon said it monitors evolving laws covering e-commerce, advertising, consumer protection, data, and product information, remains subject to regulatory reviews and open investigations involving its stores, fulfillment network, Prime, and AWS, and mitigates jurisdiction-specific requirements by using PRC-licensed third parties for certain China technology services and providing marketing and logistics tools through a compliant India marketplace structure involving an indirect minority interest in a third-party seller.

Apple Inc.

1. Most Reported Issue
Regulatory Issues in Hardware and Chips - Export Controls and Sanctions: Apple faced minimal direct exposure to China’s newly announced 34% U.S.-import tariff because its iPhones are primarily manufactured in China, but CFRA expected indirect risks from consumer backlash—especially amid two years of declining Chinese revenue—and possible retaliatory tariffs, while Chinese customs and equipment restrictions reportedly hindered Foxconn’s efforts to expand Apple’s supply chain in India; separately, President Trump said electronics remain subject to existing 20% fentanyl tariffs and could be covered by forthcoming national-security investigations into semiconductors and the broader electronics supply chain.
[4 News]
2. Biggest Risk
Regulatory Issues in E-commerce - Platforms, Competition, and Seller Governance: Regulatory scrutiny under the EU DMA and proposed Australian digital-market rules could impose substantial software, compliance, and operational costs on Apple, constrain control over its platforms, divert resources from innovation, and potentially disrupt established business models and profitability.
[4 News]
3. Most Uncertain Issue
Regulatory Issues in Hardware and Chips - Export Controls and Sanctions: Apple faces minimal direct exposure to the announced China tariffs, but potential consumer backlash, retaliatory tariffs, supply-chain disruptions affecting its India expansion, and a pending U.S. electronics supply-chain investigation create uncertainty about the eventual business impact.
[4 News]

Company's Response:
  • Regulatory Issues in Hardware and Chips - Export Controls and Sanctions: On March 14, 2025, Apple reinforced supply-chain oversight by requiring suppliers to maintain current, unaltered material test reports from ISO/IEC 17025-accredited laboratories and to obtain Apple’s prior written approval—after notifying Apple Global Supply Managers and the Environmental Team—before changing chemical formulations, manufacturing processes, sites, or production lines, with additional compliance testing where required.
  • Regulatory Issues in E-commerce - Platforms, Competition, and Seller Governance: Apple is responding to EU Digital Markets Act scrutiny by processing more than 100 developer requests and undertaking substantial software modifications, while raising concerns that measures such as Android compatibility for AirDrop could weaken security and ecosystem integrity and strain regulatory and engineering resources; it must also prepare for potential fines, higher compliance costs and Australia’s proposed service-specific obligations.

Meta Platforms Inc.

1. Most Reported Issue
Regulatory Issues in Advertising - Truthfulness and Substantiation: Meta faces heightened truthfulness, substantiation and brand-safety pressures as it labels photorealistic AI content and curbs misinformation ahead of Australia’s 2025 election, while its move away from fact-checking increases advertiser concerns about inaccurate or harmful contexts and potential budget diversion; separately, Meta’s ad policies have been challenged over allegedly erroneous or inadequately justified rejections of sexual-health advertisements, although it said one UTI-treatment ad violated prescription-drug rules and another was mistakenly blocked for nudity.
[10 News]
2. Biggest Risk
Regulatory Issues in Social Media - Misinformation and Disinformation: Meta’s reduced fact-checking and moderation may allow misinformation and disinformation to proliferate, increasing regulatory exposure—including potential EU fines of up to 6% of annual global revenue—while risking advertiser reassessment, user defection and reputational damage.
[8 News]
3. Most Uncertain Issue
Regulatory Issues in Advertising - Truthfulness and Substantiation: The reports describe ongoing and potential regulatory pressures, misleading-content and ad-policy concerns, and possible advertiser repercussions for Meta, but do not establish a definite outcome for its truthfulness and substantiation obligations.
[10 News]

Company's Response:
  • Regulatory Issues in Advertising - Truthfulness and Substantiation: The reports state that Meta’s Facebook platform has experienced rollbacks in content-moderation policies, intensifying advertiser concerns about brand safety, while providing no specific Meta mitigation measures and noting that Acast positions podcasting as a brand-safe alternative with measurable attribution and ROAS.
  • Regulatory Issues in Social Media - Misinformation and Disinformation: In January 2025, Meta announced the removal of its fact-checking program, while continuing to face European Commission inquiries into Facebook and Instagram under the Digital Services Act concerning elections, content reporting and appeals, political-content recommendations, deceptive advertising and disinformation, with potential penalties and required changes to business practices.

Microsoft Corp.

1. Most Reported Issue
Regulatory Issues in Hardware and Chips - Export Controls and Sanctions: The reports identify no direct export-control or sanctions impact on Microsoft Corp.; they mention Microsoft only as a software vendor whose support AMD relies on for software running on AMD products and as a supporter of open-source security efforts.
[9 News]
2. Biggest Risk
Regulatory Issues in AI - Risk Classification and Compliance Obligations: Microsoft is directly exposed to AI risk-classification and compliance obligations through its Responsible AI Framework, AI chatbot-related risks, and inclusion among companies affected by evolving testing and transparency rules, potentially increasing compliance costs and legal exposure.
[4 News]
3. Most Uncertain Issue
Regulatory Issues in Hardware and Chips - Export Controls and Sanctions: The reports mention export regulations only as a risk to AMD and provide no direct information about export-control or sanctions effects on Microsoft, leaving the outcome for Microsoft totally uncertain.
[9 News]

Company's Response:
  • Regulatory Issues in Hardware and Chips - Export Controls and Sanctions: In its January 29, 2025 Form 10-Q, Microsoft disclosed that it limits products, services, investments, and supply-chain integration in accordance with U.S., EU, and other sanctions, export controls, import controls, and supply-chain regulations, while warning that conflicts such as the Ukraine war could trigger rapidly changing restrictions and that noncompliance could lead to fines, operational delays, reputational harm, lost revenue, loss of export privileges, or criminal sanctions.
  • Regulatory Issues in AI - Risk Classification and Compliance Obligations: Microsoft is addressing AI-related regulatory and liability risks by applying its Responsible AI Standards with defined governance and oversight, using human review where necessary, and assessing the potential effects of flawed or biased algorithms, harmful outputs, inadequate deployment practices, and evolving requirements such as the EU AI Act, U.S. AI Executive Order, and data-protection and consumer-protection laws across Microsoft- and OpenAI-developed AI integrated into its products and customer solutions.

NVIDIA Corp.

1. Most Reported Issue
Regulatory Issues in Hardware and Chips - Export Controls and Sanctions: U.S. export controls that banned NVIDIA’s A100/H100 chips to China in October 2022, extended to its China-specific A800/H800 in October 2023 and effective in April 2024, were tightened further in April 2025 to require licenses for the H20 and potentially broader AI-chip exports under proposed “AI diffusion” rules, prompting NVIDIA to halt H20 shipments, record an approximately $5.5 billion charge, face lost Chinese demand and stronger competition from Huawei and other domestic suppliers, and warn that the measures threaten global innovation and could damage its business and U.S. competitiveness.
[14 News]
2. Biggest Risk
Regulatory Issues in Hardware and Chips - Export Controls and Sanctions: U.S. export controls have halted or restricted NVIDIA’s H20 and other AI-chip shipments to China, prompting an approximately $5.5 billion charge and risking significant lost sales and market share as Chinese customers shift toward domestic alternatives.
[14 News]
3. Most Uncertain Issue
Regulatory Issues in Hardware and Chips - Export Controls and Sanctions: NVIDIA’s H20 export licensing requirement, halted China shipments, and approximately $5.5 billion charge are already known, but potential additional restrictions, licensing outcomes, and compliance implications remain uncertain.
[14 News]

Company's Response:
  • Regulatory Issues in Hardware and Chips - Export Controls and Sanctions: Following the 2022 controls, NVIDIA relocated certain testing, validation, supply, and distribution operations out of China and Hong Kong, expanded its Data Center portfolio with solutions not requiring a license or advance shipment notice, and stated it would seek customer-specific licenses for restricted products while managing the associated time-consuming and potentially onerous NAC and D1/D4-country processes, including the H20 licensing requirement communicated on April 9, 2025.

Tesla Inc.

1. Most Reported Issue
Regulatory Issues in Hardware and Chips - Product Safety and Certification: On January 7, 2025, the U.S. National Highway Traffic Safety Administration’s Office of Defects Investigation opened a probe into Tesla’s Smart Summon and Actually Smart Summon features after four Actually Smart Summon crashes involving failures to detect objects or parked vehicles and 12 additional Smart Summon-related crashes, while noting users had too little reaction time and Tesla had not reported crashes as required, increasing regulatory and product-safety scrutiny of the technology.
[1 News]
2. Biggest Risk
Regulatory Issues in Hardware and Chips - Product Safety and Certification: NHTSA’s investigation into Tesla’s Smart Summon and Actually Smart Summon features, involving multiple reported crashes and alleged failures to report incidents, creates a medium product-safety and regulatory risk with potential financial impact from compliance actions and related costs.
[1 News]
3. Most Uncertain Issue
Regulatory Issues in Hardware and Chips - Product Safety and Certification: The outcome for Tesla is highly uncertain because NHTSA is investigating multiple Smart Summon-related crashes and Tesla has not yet provided a response or reported a regulatory resolution.
[1 News]

Company's Response:
  • Regulatory Issues in Hardware and Chips - Product Safety and Certification: As of January 7, 2025, Tesla had not publicly responded to the investigation, did not immediately reply to a request for comment, and had not reported the cited crashes despite the regulator’s stated reporting requirements, with no mitigation or corrective plan disclosed in the reports.
